action_criteria.expected_evidence: Evans index 0.42 with DESH, callosal angle 65 degrees, temporal horn enlargement, patent aqueduct with flow void, Fazekas 2, MTA 2, no obstructing lesion or subdural collection
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI with the iNPH markers: Evans index, callosal angle, temporal horns, DESH, aqueduct, periventricular signal and hippocampi
action_criteria.rationale: The outside report of enlarged ventricles needs measurement of the markers and exclusion of an obstructing lesion or subdural collection after his falls with head injury.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, electrolytes, renal function, TSH and vitamin B12; RPR and HIV non-reactive
action_criteria.label: Targeted labs for reversible contributors
action_criteria.rationale: Nothing in his history points to a metabolic or infectious contributor, so a blood screen is good practice but does not change the iNPH decision.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 38 s with rollator, 10-m walk 32 s in 34 steps, 180-degree turn in 9 steps, magnetic gait with impaired postural reflexes
action_criteria.label: Baseline timed gait assessment before the tap
action_criteria.rationale: His TUG and 10-m walk must be timed before CSF is removed, with the rollator he always uses, so the post-tap change can be measured.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 18/30 with executive, visuospatial and retrieval deficits and cueing benefit
action_criteria.label: Bedside cognitive screen
action_criteria.rationale: A MoCA documents his frontal-subcortical deficits and gives a cognitive baseline to repeat after the tap.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Opening pressure 15 cmH2O, normal cells, protein and glucose; 45 mL removed; TUG 38 to 24 s (37%) at 24 hours
action_criteria.label: CSF tap test: opening pressure, routine CSF and removal of 30-50 mL
action_criteria.rationale: Removing 45 mL with normal opening pressure and normal CSF content tests whether his gait improves when CSF is drained.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 28 s at 2 hours and 24 s at 24 hours (37% faster), 10-m walk 21 s (34% faster), MoCA 21/30
action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating his rollator-assisted TUG and 10-m walk at 2 and 24 hours after the 45 mL tap shows whether his gait responds to CSF removal.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the syndrome to normal ageing or deconditioning in a patient with ventriculomegaly, DESH and an objective tap response
Do not stop aspirin for the lumbar tap
Do not withhold shunt referral on the grounds of age alone
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 37% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]; age 80 and stable coronary disease are not by themselves contraindications
Continue aspirin 81 mg through the lumbar tap; low-dose aspirin alone does not require interruption before lumbar puncture [ASRA_2025]
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: He has had no seizures or fluctuating awareness, so an EEG does not address his progressive gait and cognitive syndrome.
His falls happened while walking or turning without loss of consciousness or palpitations, so an ECG does not explain them.
His coronary disease is stable and asymptomatic, and an echocardiogram does not inform the iNPH work-up or the tap test.
MRI is available and measures the callosal angle, DESH and hippocampi that CT cannot assess as well.
His falls are gait falls without syncope or palpitations, so ambulatory rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test.
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are.
A three-year course without rapid decline, fever or inflammatory features gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious CSF assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 white matter change in a hypertensive former smoker may contribute, but ventriculomegaly with DESH and a 37% TUG improvement after the tap are not explained by small-vessel disease.
No tremor or rigidity, full vertical gaze and a gait that improves after CSF removal argue against parkinsonism.
His brother had Alzheimer's disease, but gait came first, recall improves with cueing, MTA is 2 (within the range for age 80) and gait and MoCA improve after the tap.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventricles markedly disproportionate to cortical volume loss, tight high-convexity sulci and an acute callosal angle argue against ex-vacuo enlargement.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic) communicating hydrocephalus
differential.key_features: Gait decline preceded his falls by two years, there is no history of meningitis or haemorrhage, and the MRI shows no subdural collection.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH requires an insidious gait disturbance after age 40, progressing over at least 3 to 6 months without an antecedent cause, plus cognitive or urinary symptoms; he has all three over three years [Relkin_2005]
MRI shows Evans index 0.42 with both DESH components, a callosal angle of 65 degrees and temporal horn enlargement, with no obstructing lesion [Relkin_2005]
Opening pressure 15 cmH2O with normal CSF content meets the pressure criterion [Relkin_2005]

After removal of 45 mL, TUG fell from 38 to 24 s (37%) at 24 hours and the 10-m walk from 32 to 21 s; an improvement of 10% or more in TUG is a commonly used positive threshold, though no guideline sets a single cut-off
The tap test has a sensitivity of 26% to 61% and a PPV of 73% to 100%, so a clear response supports shunting while a negative tap would not have excluded it [Marmarou_2005]
Shunting is graded possibly effective by the AAN [Halperin_2015]; at 80 with stable coronary disease he remains a surgical candidate, and age alone is not a contraindication

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

patient.history_present_illness: An 80-year-old retired bank manager with CAD (CABG 12 years ago), hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for evaluation of progressive gait dysfunction, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline over the past three years. His wife reports that his walking gradually became slower and more shuffling approximately three years ago. He initially dismissed this as 'getting old.' Over the past year his gait has worsened significantly: he has a wide-based shuffling walk and has had four falls while walking or turning, none with loss of consciousness or palpitations, including one that caused a scalp laceration requiring sutures. He now uses a rollator walker full-time and cannot ambulate safely without it. He requires assistance to get dressed due to slow, clumsy movements. Urinary incontinence has been present for approximately two years: he has two to three episodes of urge incontinence per week despite timed voiding strategies. His wife has noticed progressive cognitive deterioration: he cannot balance his checkbook, has become disoriented in familiar surroundings twice, and repeats the same stories in conversation. He has always been a sharp and precise man, and his cognitive decline is very distressing to his family. There is no tremor, rigidity, headache, or diplopia. A brain MRI obtained three months ago at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. His primary care physician referred him to neurology for progressive gait difficulty with memory decline and urinary incontinence.
